title: Consumers are participants in the information system: Health literacy, portals, personal health records, and telehealth
overview: Consumer informatics examines health information and technology from the patient or consumer perspective. This week considers how health literacy, accessible design, portals, personal health records, and telehealth shape access, understanding, engagement, and action—and how HIM responsibilities help protect information quality, meaning, trust, and use.
objectives: Explain consumer informatics from the patient or consumer perspective.
Explain how health literacy affects people’s ability to find, understand, and use health information.
Distinguish a patient portal from a personal health record (PHR).
Use the Access → Understand → Engage → Act framework to explain how consumer-facing systems support information use and action.
Describe HIM responsibilities for protecting information quality, meaning, trust, and use in consumer-facing systems.

concepts.name: HIM responsibilities in consumer informatics
concepts.definition: Responsibilities include explaining system purpose and limits; supporting definitions, standards, terminology, mapping, and consistent interpretation; checking information quality; supporting privacy, security, appropriate access, auditability, and responsible disclosure; and improving workflow through feedback, testing, training, monitoring, and root-cause correction.

concepts.name: Information quality and trust principles
concepts.definition: Principles grouped as purpose and fit; data and meaning; access and trust; and workflow and adoption. Controls include workflow fit, definitions, metadata, validation, mapping, policy, role-based access, authentication, logs, user testing, training, monitoring, and improvement.

sections.body: Consumer informatics studies health information and technology from the patient or consumer perspective. This perspective focuses attention on whether people can access information, understand it, communicate about it, and use it. Health literacy affects whether people can find, understand, and use health information; therefore, a consumer-facing service must be considered not only in terms of what it makes available, but also in terms of whether people can make sense of and act on it. Consumer tools can improve access and engagement, but poorly designed tools can also widen disparities. Accessible language, visuals, translation, and usability are safety features, not merely presentation choices. Telehealth is remote delivery, communication, monitoring, or support.
sections.title: Consumer informatics puts the patient or consumer perspective in view

sections.body: A patient portal is an organizational service connected to a provider’s system. Access is organization-managed, and typical uses include results, appointments, messages, and forms. A personal health record (PHR), in contrast, is an electronic or paper record maintained by or for the individual. It may combine information from several sources under the individual’s control; typical uses include personal history, medications, directives, and tracking. To compare the two, identify who manages the record or service, what system or sources it connects to, and what it is typically used for. For example, a patient may use a portal to read results, send a message, schedule an appointment, and share information with an authorized caregiver. A PHR may bring together information from several sources under the individual’s control.
sections.title: Distinguish an organization-managed portal from an individual-managed PHR

sections.body: The framework organizes a consumer-facing information task into four linked stages. Access means giving the person appropriate access to information. Understand means presenting that information in a form the person can understand. Engage means supporting communication and shared decisions. Act means enabling a safe next step or self-management action. Use the sequence to examine what happens, who is responsible, and where control is needed at each point. A service can make information available yet still fall short if it is not understandable, does not support communication, or does not enable a safe next step.
sections.title: Trace consumer information use through Access → Understand → Engage → Act

sections.body:
The quality and governance principles group the work into four areas. Purpose and fit asks whether the system supports its intended users, work, outputs, and decisions; scope, workflow fit, and measurable objectives provide ways to examine this. Data and meaning concerns whether information is complete, valid, consistent, timely, and understood; definitions, metadata, validation, and mapping are relevant controls. Access and trust concerns privacy, security, integrity, and auditability, supported by policy, role-based access, authentication, and logs. Workflow and adoption concerns whether people can use information safely and effectively, with user testing, training, monitoring, and improvement as supporting practices.

HIM professionals connect system purpose to trustworthy information work. They explain the system’s users, inputs, outputs, decisions, and limits; support definitions, standards, terminology, mapping, and consistent interpretation; check identity, completeness, accuracy, validity, timeliness, and consistency; support privacy, security, appropriate access, auditability, and responsible disclosure; and improve workflow using feedback, testing, training, monitoring, and root-cause correction. Together, these responsibilities protect the quality, meaning, trust, and use of information in consumer-facing systems.

activities.title: Follow the information-use sequence
activities.prompt: Place the framework stages in order, from providing access to enabling a next step.

activities.title: Assessing a consumer-facing information service
activities.prompt: Hypothetical situation: A team is reviewing a consumer-facing service. It provides access to information, but the information is difficult for people to understand and the service offers no support for communication or a safe next step. Which framework-based assessment best identifies the gaps?
activities.debrief: The framework distinguishes access from understanding, engagement, and action. Making information available addresses Access, but the situation describes gaps in the other stages.
options: The service supports all four stages because information is available.
Access is addressed, but Understand, Engage, and Act still need attention.
Only Act matters because the service is intended for consumers.
The framework applies only to personal health records, not other consumer-facing services.

items.text: Check whether the system supports intended users, work, outputs, and decisions.

activities.prompt: Classify each control under the principle area it most directly supports.
activities.feedback: The four areas distinguish system purpose, information meaning, access and trust controls, and the support needed for safe workflow and adoption.

activities.title: Trace a consumer information task
activities.answer: A strong response applies the four stages in sequence and connects the selected task to relevant HIM responsibilities, such as checking information quality, supporting appropriate access, or improving workflow through feedback and testing.
